zug-bug:
How to tie a Zug Bug. Cliff Zug's peacock nymph has been fooling trout since the nineteen-thirties. The peacock herl glows in the water, and the short mallard wing case gives it a buggy profile.

You'll need a two-X-long nymph hook, size ten to sixteen. Black eight-oh thread. Peacock sword fibers for the tail, oval silver tinsel for the rib, peacock herl for the body, a brown hen feather for the beard, and mallard flank for the wing case.

Step one. At the bend, tie in a short tail of peacock sword fibers, then the silver tinsel.

Step two. Wind a full peacock herl body forward, and rib it with the tinsel.

Step three. Turn the fly over and tie a small beard of brown hen fibers underneath, just behind the eye.

Step four. On top, tie in a slip of mallard flank as the wing case, trim it to about a third of the body length, and whip finish.

Dead-drift it or swing it. It's a great general nymph for trout and panfish.

psycho-prince:
How to tie a Psycho Prince. Greg Senyo gave the classic Prince Nymph a flashy makeover, with Ice Dub and brightly colored biot wings. It's a top attractor for trout, and steelhead in the Great Lakes tributaries love it too.

You'll need a nymph hook, size twelve to eighteen. A gold bead. Black eight-oh thread. Goose biots for the tail, Ice Dub or tinsel for the body, colored goose biots for the wings, and Ice Dub for the collar.

Step one. Slide on the bead, start the thread, and tie in two biots at the bend as a forked tail.

Step two. Build a flashy body of Ice Dub or tinsel up to about a quarter shank behind the bead.

Step three. Tie two colored biots on top, flared outward in a V, as the wings.

Step four. Dub a small Ice Dub collar behind the bead and whip finish.

Fish it as an attractor nymph. It also works well on steelhead tributaries.

renegade:
How to tie a Renegade. Taylor Williams created this Idaho attractor with a hackle at each end of a peacock body. It floats well, and when it sinks, it swims like a wet fly. Either way, trout eat it.

You'll need a standard dry hook, size ten to sixteen. Black eight-oh thread. Flat gold tinsel for the tag, a brown rooster hackle for the rear, peacock herl for the body, and a white rooster hackle for the front.

Step one. At the bend, wrap a small tag of flat gold tinsel.

Step two. Just in front of the tag, tie in a brown hackle and wind a few turns.

Step three. Wrap a full peacock herl body forward.

Step four. At the front, wind a white hackle, tie it off and whip finish.

Fish it dry, or let it sink and swing it as a wet fly at the end of the drift.

royal-coachman:
How to tie a Royal Coachman. This flashy American classic dates back to the eighteen-seventies. It doesn't imitate any insect, but its white wings and red band have been drawing strikes in mountain streams for generations.

You'll need a standard dry hook, size ten to sixteen. Black eight-oh thread. Golden pheasant tippets for the tail, peacock herl and red floss for the body, white duck quill slips for the wings, and a brown rooster hackle.

Step one. A third back from the eye, tie in two slips of white duck quill, upright and divided.

Step two. At the bend, tie in a tail of golden pheasant tippets.

Step three. Wind a band of peacock herl, then a band of red floss, then another band of peacock herl up to the wings.

Step four. Wind the brown hackle behind and in front of the wings, and whip finish.

It's an attractor for fast mountain streams, where trout have to decide quickly.

humpy:
How to tie a Humpy. This western classic, also called the Goofus Bug, uses one bunch of deer hair for both the hump and the wings. It's tricky to measure the first few times, but it floats in the roughest water.

You'll need a standard dry hook, size ten to eighteen. Yellow or red six-oh thread. Moose hair for the tail, deer hair for the back and wings, floss for the underbody, and one brown and one grizzly hackle.

Step one. At the bend, tie in a tail of moose hair about as long as the shank.

Step two. Tie in a bunch of deer hair with the tips pointing back. Measure it so the tips will reach past the front of the body, since they'll become the wings.

Step three. Build a floss underbody, then pull the deer hair forward over it, and tie it down to form the hump.

Step four. Stand the hair tips up, and divide them into two wings.

Step five. Wind the brown and grizzly hackles around the wings, and whip finish.

Fish it in fast pocket water, where you need a fly that won't sink.

hornberg:
How to tie a Hornberg. Frank Hornberg's odd little fly works two ways: skate it on top like a caddis, then let it sink and strip it back like a minnow. It's been a favorite in Maine and the Midwest for decades.

You'll need a two-X-long streamer hook, size six to twelve. Black six-oh thread. Flat silver tinsel for the body, yellow hackle tips for the underwing, mallard flank for the wing, jungle cock for optional cheeks, and a grizzly hackle for the collar.

Step one. Wrap a smooth, flat silver tinsel body.

Step two. On top, tie in a pair of yellow hackle tips as the underwing.

Step three. Fold a mallard flank feather around the hackle tips as the wing, and add jungle cock cheeks if you have them.

Step four. Wind a grizzly hackle collar in front of the wing, and whip finish.

Skate it on the surface first, then let it sink and strip it back like a minnow.

intruder:
How to tie an Intruder. Ed Ward's big steelhead fly looks huge in the water but sheds water on the cast. It's built on a shank with a trailing hook, so it stays light and hooks fish well.

You'll need an intruder shank and a trailing hook on a braided loop. Strong GSP thread. Dubbing and hackle for the rear hub, ostrich, marabou and flash for the collars, and optional dumbbell eyes.

Step one. Tie the braided loop onto the shank and attach the trailing hook.

Step two. At the rear of the shank, build a small ball of dubbing, and wind a hackle in front of it. That hub props the rest of the fly open.

Step three. Move to the front and wind collars of ostrich and marabou, adding flash between them.

Step four. Tie off and whip finish.

Swing it on a sink-tip for winter steelhead.

kreelex:
How to tie a Kreelex. Chuck Kraft's all-flash minnow is nothing but gold and silver Flashabou and a pair of eyes. In clear water it flashes like a fleeing baitfish, and smallmouth and trout chase it down.

You'll need a streamer hook, size two to six. Red three-oh thread. Gold and silver Flashabou, and stick-on eyes with glue.

Step one. Tie a bunch of silver Flashabou on top of the shank and another underneath, then add a bunch of gold on top.

Step two. Tie the bunches in facing forward, then fold them back and tie them down, so the head is fuller.

Step three. Glue on a pair of eyes, and coat the head.

Strip it fast for smallmouth bass and trout in clear rivers.

thin-mint:
How to tie a Thin Mint. This woolly bugger variation blends black, olive and brown marabou into a mottled tail that looks great in the water. It's a reliable producer in both rivers and lakes.

You'll need a two-X-long streamer hook, size six to twelve. A gold bead. Olive six-oh thread. Black, olive and brown marabou with a little flash for the tail, peacock or olive chenille for the body, and a brown saddle hackle.

Step one. Slide on the bead and start the thread. At the bend, tie in a tail of mixed black, olive and brown marabou with a few strands of flash.

Step two. Tie in the hackle and the chenille. Wind the chenille body forward, then palmer the hackle through it.

Step three. Tie off and whip finish behind the bead.

Strip it or dead-drift it in rivers and lakes.

catskill-adams:
How to tie a Catskill Adams. Leonard Halladay tied the first Adams in Michigan in nineteen-twenty-two, and it's still one of the best grey mayfly patterns there is. This is the original style, with hackle-tip wings.

You'll need a standard dry hook, size twelve to twenty. Black eight-oh thread. Grizzly hen hackle tips for the wings, brown and grizzly fibers for the tail, muskrat or grey dubbing, and one brown and one grizzly rooster hackle.

Step one. A third back from the eye, tie in two grizzly hackle tips, upright and divided.

Step two. At the bend, tie in a tail of mixed brown and grizzly fibers.

Step three. Dub a slim grey body up to the wings.

Step four. Wind both hackles together, behind and in front of the wings, and whip finish.

It's a general grey mayfly. Fish it to rising trout on riffles and flats.
